cpu_layers.name: Package / Substrate
cpu_layers.description: The green PCB that carries the die and routes its thousands of connections out to the socket contacts. It also distributes power to the die through a dense grid of vias.

cpu_layers.name: Integrated Heat Spreader
cpu_layers.description: The nickel-plated copper lid soldered or pasted over the die. It spreads concentrated heat from a small die across a larger surface the cooler can contact.

cpu_layers.name: Silicon Die
cpu_layers.description: The actual processor: a single piece of patterned silicon holding cores, cache, memory controller and interconnect. Everything above this layer exists to power it, cool it, and connect it.

cpu_layers.name: Cores
cpu_layers.description: Independent execution engines. Each has its own front-end, execution units, and private L1/L2 cache. The OS scheduler assigns threads to cores -- the decision several VOIDTUNE tweaks influence.

cpu_layers.name: Cache Hierarchy
cpu_layers.description: Small, fast memory close to the execution units. L1 is fastest and smallest, L3 is shared across cores. A cache miss that reaches main memory costs roughly two orders of magnitude more time than an L1 hit.

cpu_layers.name: Execution Units
cpu_layers.description: The circuits that actually compute: integer ALUs, floating-point and vector units, load/store units. A single core has several, so independent instructions can execute in the same cycle.

cpu_layers.name: Registers
cpu_layers.description: The fastest storage in the machine -- a few dozen named slots (rax, rsi, ...) read and written in a single cycle. Compilers work hard to keep hot values here rather than in memory.

cpu_layers.name: Transistors
cpu_layers.description: The switches everything above is built from. Billions of them, each a few nanometres across, forming the logic gates that implement every instruction.

pipeline.name: Fetch
pipeline.description: The core reads the next instruction from the L1 instruction cache, at the address held in the program counter. A branch predictor guesses where execution goes next so the pipeline never sits idle waiting to find out.

pipeline.name: Decode
pipeline.description: The x86 instruction is translated into one or more internal micro-operations the execution units understand. This is where a variable-length CISC instruction becomes fixed-width internal work.

pipeline.name: Execute
pipeline.description: Micro-operations are dispatched to whichever execution unit is free -- ALU, FPU, load/store. Out-of-order execution means instructions can run in a different order than written, as long as the visible result is identical.

pipeline.name: Writeback
pipeline.description: Results are committed to the architectural registers or memory, in original program order. Retirement in order is what makes out-of-order execution safe.

units.name: Control Unit
units.description: Sequences the pipeline: decides what is fetched, when micro-ops issue, and how the core responds to branches, interrupts and stalls.

units.name: ALU
units.description: Arithmetic Logic Unit -- integer add, subtract, compare, bitwise operations. The workhorse for ordinary code.

units.name: FPU / Vector
units.description: Floating-point and SIMD units. Executes one operation across many values at once (SSE/AVX), which is why vectorized code can be several times faster.

units.name: L1 Cache
units.description: Split into instruction and data halves, private per core, roughly 4-5 cycle latency. The first place any memory access is looked for.

units.name: L2 Cache
units.description: Larger, private per core, ~14 cycles. Catches what misses L1.

units.name: L3 Cache
units.description: Shared across all cores, tens of megabytes, ~40+ cycles. Also the coherence point between cores.

units.name: Memory Controller
units.description: On-die since the mid-2000s. Talks directly to the DIMMs, which removed the old front-side-bus bottleneck between CPU and RAM.

units.name: Register File
units.description: The named registers plus a much larger pool of physical registers used for renaming, which is what allows out-of-order execution without false dependencies.

software_stack.name: VOIDTUNE
software_stack.description: A user-space Windows application. It does not patch the kernel or load a driver -- it changes documented OS configuration (registry values, service start types, power plan settings) and lets Windows apply the consequences.
software_stack.reaches: Writes configuration that the OS reads.

software_stack.name: Application
software_stack.description: Ordinary user-mode programs: games, browsers, VOIDTUNE itself. They cannot touch hardware directly -- the CPU runs them in a restricted privilege level (ring 3) where privileged instructions fault.
software_stack.reaches: Calls into the OS for anything privileged.

software_stack.name: Operating System / Win32
software_stack.description: The API surface applications actually call. Windows exposes subsystems (Win32, registry, scheduler policy) that translate ordinary calls into kernel requests.

software_stack.name: System Call Boundary
software_stack.description: The privilege transition. A syscall instruction switches the CPU from user mode to kernel mode at a fixed, controlled entry point -- the only legal way into the kernel.

software_stack.name: Kernel
software_stack.description: Owns the scheduler, memory manager, and drivers. This is where a decision like 'which core runs this thread' is actually made, and where most of VOIDTUNE's settings take effect.

software_stack.name: CPU Instructions
software_stack.description: Everything above compiles down to machine instructions. Privileged ones (writing control registers, MSRs, port I/O) only execute in kernel mode.

software_stack.name: Hardware
software_stack.description: The physical components. Voltage, clocks, cache, memory buses -- the layer where a scheduling or power decision made six layers up becomes a measurable difference in frame time.
